plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.3.3
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a polar rectangle R, the fundamental building block for polar double integration. The region R is bounded by two circular arcs r = 1.5 and r = 2 (solid blue curves) and two rays theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4 (dashed red lines), forming a curved quadrilateral shaded in light blue and labeled R. The figure introduces the polar rectangle as the analogue of the Cartesian rectangle for setting up double integrals in polar coordinates, showing how its curved sides arise from the constant-r and constant-theta boundary conditions.

interactionPlan.concept: A polar rectangle is a region bounded by two constant-radius arcs and two constant-angle rays, so its double-integral limits are rectangular in the variables r and θ even though the shape is curved in the plane.
elements: polar origin at the lower left
black horizontal polar axis extending right from the origin
dashed red ray from the origin labeled θ = π/6
dashed red ray from the origin labeled θ = π/4
solid blue inner circular arc labeled r = 1.5
solid blue outer circular arc labeled r = 2
light blue shaded polar rectangle R between the two arcs and two rays
large label R centered inside the shaded region
highlighted representative polar integration slice
display of polar bounds π/6 ≤ θ ≤ π/4 and 1.5 ≤ r ≤ 2
display of the corresponding iterated integral order

interactions.label: Integration order
interactions.teaches: The same polar rectangle can be swept either by radial segments at fixed θ or by circular arc strips at fixed r, giving equivalent orders of polar integration

interactions.label: Move the polar slice
interactions.teaches: A polar integration slice holds one coordinate fixed while the other coordinate runs between constant bounds: r from 1.5 to 2 or θ from π/6 to π/4

demo_steps.title: Identify the four polar boundaries
demo_steps.narration: The blue curves are constant-r boundaries, r = 1.5 and r = 2. The red dashed rays are constant-θ boundaries, θ = π/6 and θ = π/4.

demo_steps.title: Sweep with fixed θ
demo_steps.narration: With order dr then dθ, the highlighted slice is a radial segment: θ is fixed while r runs from the inner arc to the outer arc. Moving the slider changes the angle of the slice between π/6 and π/4.

demo_steps.title: Reverse the order
demo_steps.narration: Switching the order makes the highlighted slice a circular arc strip: r is fixed while θ runs from π/6 to π/4. The numerical bounds stay constant because this region is rectangular in polar coordinates.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The region looks curved in the xy-plane, but in polar coordinates it is simply the rectangle 1.5 ≤ r ≤ 2 and π/6 ≤ θ ≤ π/4.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Place the polar origin near the lower left with a black horizontal polar axis along the bottom. Draw two dashed red rays from the origin, the lower one at θ = π/6 and the upper one at θ = π/4, with italic math labels near the rays. Draw two thick solid blue circular arcs centered at the origin, the inner labeled r = 1.5 and the outer labeled r = 2. Shade only the curved quadrilateral between the two arcs and two rays in light blue, and put a large italic R inside. In dr then dθ mode, show a darker highlighted radial segment spanning from r = 1.5 to r = 2 at the slider-selected angle. In dθ then dr mode, show a darker highlighted circular arc strip at the slider-selected radius spanning from θ = π/6 to θ = π/4. Display the matching integral limits near the figure.
